implementation_notes: Ktor models the chain as a pipeline of ordered phases: ApplicationCallPipeline declares Setup, Monitoring, Plugins, Call and Fallback, a plugin installs itself with pipeline.intercept(ApplicationCallPipeline.Plugins) { ... }, and proceed() delegates to the next interceptor so that omitting the call short-circuits the request. The FilterManager and FilterChain roles are the pipeline and its interceptor list, and interception positions have names rather than magic numbers. On the JVM a Spring HandlerInterceptor is an equally idiomatic alternative; hand-writing a Filter interface on top of Ktor adds nothing to the built-in pipeline.
pitfalls: An interceptor that never calls proceed() stalls the call until the client times out; every path must proceed or respond.
Plugins intercepting the same phase run in installation order, so the order of install(...) calls is part of the chain contract.
Blocking work inside an interceptor occupies a dispatcher thread - wrap it in withContext(Dispatchers.IO) or the whole call pipeline loses throughput.
